# Baruch Chapter 6 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
## [The Letter of Jeremiah]

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Baruch 6

---

**1** A copy of the letter that Jeremiah sent to those who were about to be led captive to Babylon by the king of the Babylonians, to give them the message that God had commanded him.

**2** Because of the sins that you have committed before God, you will be led away as captives to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians.

**3** When you arrive in Babylon you will remain there for many years, for a long time — up to seven generations; after that I will bring you back from there in peace.

**4** And now in Babylon you will see gods made of silver and gold and wood, carried on shoulders, filling the nations with awe.

**5** Beware, therefore, of becoming like those foreigners; do not let fear of them take hold of you

**6** when you see the crowds before and behind them, worshipping them. But say in your heart: It is you, O Lord, who must be worshipped.

**7** For my angel is with you, and he is watching over your souls.

**8** Their tongues have been polished smooth by a craftsman; they themselves are overlaid with gold and silver; but they are false and cannot speak.

**9** People bring gold as an offering to them as they would adorn a girl who loves jewelry —

**10** but the priests take the gold and silver from their gods and spend it on themselves.

**11** They even give some of it to prostitutes on the temple rooftop, and they clothe these wooden, silvered, and gilded gods with garments like human beings.

**12** Yet these gods cannot save themselves from rust and moths, though they are wrapped in purple robes.

**13** Their faces must be wiped on account of the thick dust of the temple that settles upon them.

**14** He who cannot put to death anyone who wrongs him wields a scepter like a judge over a land;

**15** he has a dagger in his right hand and an axe; but he cannot deliver himself from war and brigands.

**16** From this it is evident that they are not gods; so do not fear them.

**17** For just as a vessel a man uses becomes useless when it is broken, so are their gods: when they have been set up in temples, their eyes are filled with dust raised by the feet of those who enter.

**18** And just as the gates are locked on every side against anyone who has offended a king, condemned to death, so the priests secure the temples with doors, bolts, and bars, in case they are plundered by robbers.

**19** They light more lamps for them than they light for themselves, though the gods cannot see a single one.

**20** They are like a wooden beam of the house; they say the hearts within them are eaten out; when creeping things from the earth devour both them and their garments, they do not feel it.

**21** Their faces are blackened by the smoke that comes from the temple.

**22** Bats and swallows and birds settle on their bodies and heads; and so do cats.

**23** From this you will know that they are not gods; so do not fear them.

**24** The gold that beautifies them — unless someone wipes off the tarnish, they will not shine; and even when they were being cast, they had no feeling.

**25** They are purchased without regard to price; there is no breath in them.

**26** Having no feet, they are carried on shoulders, displaying their own shame before all mankind; and those who serve them are humiliated as well.

**27** If they are set on the ground, they cannot rise; and if anyone tilts them over, they cannot right themselves; offerings placed before them are like offerings placed before the dead.

**28** What is sacrificed to them their priests sell and pocket; their wives also preserve some of it in brine, but give nothing to the poor or the helpless.

**29** Women in menstruation and women in childbirth touch their sacrifices; knowing therefore from these things that they are not gods, do not fear them.

**30** For how can they be called gods? Women serve as officiants at the shrines of these wooden, silvered, and golden gods.

**31** And in their temples the priests sit with torn robes, with their heads and beards shaved and their heads uncovered.

**32** They howl and cry out before their gods as people do at a funeral feast.

**33** The priests take some of their garments and dress their own wives and children in them.

**34** Whether one does good or harm to them, they cannot repay it; they can neither set up a king nor depose one.

**35** Likewise they can neither give wealth nor provide money; if one makes a vow to them and does not keep it, they will not demand an accounting.

**36** They cannot save a person from death or rescue the weak from the powerful.

**37** They cannot restore sight to the blind; they cannot deliver a person in distress.

**38** They cannot show mercy to a widow or do good to an orphan.

**39** Their wooden, gilded, and silvered gods are like the stones of the mountain; those who serve them will be put to shame.

**40** How then can anyone suppose or say that they are gods?

**41** Even the Chaldeans themselves dishonor them; for when they see a mute person unable to speak, they bring him and ask Bel to make him speak, as if Bel had understanding.

**42** Yet they themselves cannot perceive this and abandon them; for they have no sense.

**43** The women, with cords tied around them, sit in the streets burning bran as incense; and when one of them is drawn aside by a passerby who lies with her, she taunts her neighbor who has not been honored as she has, and whose cord has not been cut.

**44** Everything that is done for them is false; how then can anyone suppose or say that they are gods?

**45** They are made by craftsmen and goldsmiths; they can become nothing other than what the craftsmen intend them to be.

**46** Those who make them cannot themselves live very long; how then can the things they have made be gods?

**47** For they have left only falsehood and reproach to those who come after them.

**48** For when war and disaster come upon them, the priests take counsel among themselves about where to hide with the gods.

**49** How then can one fail to understand that they are not gods — these things that cannot save themselves from war and calamity?

**50** Since they are of wood, overlaid with silver and gold, it will be known in time that they are false; it will become plain to all nations and kings that they are not gods but the work of human hands, and that there is no work of God in them.

**51** Who then can fail to know that they are not gods?

**52** For they cannot set up a king over a land or give rain to human beings.

**53** They cannot adjudicate their own case or deliver one who is wronged; for they are without power; they are like crows between heaven and earth.

**54** When fire breaks out in the house of wooden, silvered, and gilded gods, their priests will flee and escape, while they themselves are burned there like timbers.

**55** Moreover they cannot withstand a king or enemies; how then can one accept or think that they are gods?

**56** Gods made of wood, overlaid with silver and gold, are unable to protect themselves from thieves or robbers.

**57** Anyone stronger than they will strip them of their gold and silver and the garments they wear, and go off with it; they will be powerless to help themselves.

**58** Therefore it is better to be a king showing his valor, or a household vessel that serves its owner's needs, than these false gods; better also a door of a house that protects those inside, than these false gods; better also a wooden pillar in a palace, than these false gods.

**59** For sun and moon and stars are brilliant, and when sent on their errands they are obedient.

**60** Likewise lightning, when it flashes, is widely seen; and the wind blows over every land.

**61** And when God commands the clouds to traverse the whole earth, they carry out his command.

**62** And fire, sent from above to consume mountains and forests, does what it is commanded; but these gods are not to be compared to any of them, either in appearance or in power.

**63** Therefore one must not think or say that they are gods; they are unable to give judgment or do good to human beings.

**64** Knowing then that they are not gods, do not fear them.

**65** They can neither curse kings nor bless them.

**66** They show no signs in the heavens for the nations; they neither shine like the sun nor give light like the moon.

**67** Wild animals are better off than they are, for they can flee to cover and look after themselves.

**68** So it is in no way evident to us that they are gods; therefore do not fear them.

**69** For like a scarecrow in a cucumber field that guards nothing, so are their wooden, silvered, and gilded gods.

**70** In the same way their wooden, gilded, and silvered gods are like a white thornbush in a garden, on which every bird perches; or like a corpse thrown out in the darkness.

**71** By the purple and linen that rot upon them you will know that they are not gods; and they will in the end be consumed and become a reproach in the land.

**72** Better therefore is the upright person who has no idols — for he will be far from reproach.

---

## Council Notes

**On the refrain — structural analysis:** The refrain "from this it is evident that they are not gods; so do not fear them" (and its variants) occurs at approximately the following verses: 16, 23, 29, 40, 44, 49, 51, 64, 68, 72. The variations in the refrain are deliberate and part of the satire's rhetoric — each landing with slightly different phrasing prevents mechanical repetition while preserving the structural beat.

Refrain inventory:
- v.16: "From this it is evident that they are not gods; so do not fear them."
- v.23: "From this you will know that they are not gods; so do not fear them."
- v.29: "knowing therefore from these things that they are not gods, do not fear them."
- v.40: "How then can anyone suppose or say that they are gods?"
- v.44: "Everything that is done for them is false; how then can anyone suppose or say that they are gods?"
- v.49: "How then can one fail to understand that they are not gods...?"
- v.51: "Who then can fail to know that they are not gods?"
- v.64: "Knowing then that they are not gods, do not fear them."
- v.68: "So it is in no way evident to us that they are gods; therefore do not fear them."
- v.72: Final verse — a positive conclusion, not the refrain itself.

**On v.4 — "filling the nations with awe":** EMET "inspiring awe among the nations"; LOGOS "filling the nations with awe"; PNEUMA "filling the nations with terror." Greek ekphobizonta = inspiring fear/awe. The idol-cult depends on fear. "Awe" is slightly too positive; "terror" is too extreme. Consensus: "filling the nations with awe."

**On v.20 — "they are like a wooden beam":** All agents retain the timber comparison. This metaphor is the key to the whole letter: the idol is just wood. v.54 will return to this when the priests flee but the idols burn "like timbers."

**On vv.43-44 — temple prostitution:** All agents render this passage plainly and accurately. The practice described is the Babylonian bride-of-Marduk ritual (attested in Herodotus), where women sat in the temple precincts until a stranger chose them. The satirical irony is that women compete for this "honor." PNEUMA's rendering is most vivid but all are accurate. Consensus follows LOGOS/PNEUMA closely.

**On v.58 — the triple "better than" comparison:** The three comparisons (king, household vessel, door, pillar — the Greek text has four items) are a classic wisdom rhetorical form (cf. Prov 12:9, Qoh 4:6). All agents preserve all four comparisons. PNEUMA's colloquial rendering ("a kitchen pot") is accurate but the neutral "vessel" is preferred.

**On v.67 — "wild animals":** EMET and LOGOS "wild animals"; PNEUMA "animals." The contrast is stark: creatures without reason can at least run away and survive. The idol cannot even do that. Consensus: "wild animals" for the contrast between the idol's helplessness and even irrational creation's ability to act.
